title: NimbusWorks POC - capacity & autoscale scoping

Customer provided workload profile (avg qps, token counts) and prioritized latency SLAs for interactive features. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run benchmark with sample traces, propose reserved capacity + burst plan, share security docs, schedule technical deep dive for SRE team.

warmup / cold start and KV cache behavior

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-24 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 min
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (Nimbus Head of Platform), Jara (CTO), Ethan (ML Infra), Sophie (Security)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, um we'll kick off — quick roll call?
[00:08] Mark: Hey, Mark here.
[00:10] Jara: Jara on from Nimbus.
[00:12] Ethan: Ethan, ML infra.
[00:14] Sophie: Sophie, security.
[00:16] Alex: Great. Priya and I will own technical and scope. Goal today is to scope capacity for the POC — reserved GPUs, burst strategy, autoscale and what success looks like.
[00:30] Priya: Quick agenda: go over your workload, QPS and token distribution, then sizing options (reserved vs burst), fallback policies, and bench plan.
[00:42] Mark: For context, our product is interactive code assistance, so latency at p95 matters — target under 500ms for chat-ish requests. Peak QPS is about 120 sustained, spikey peaks up to ~250 for short windows. Typical request is 120 tokens in, 40 tokens out on average.
[01:05] Alex: Helpful — and is that global or single region?
[01:09] Mark: Mostly us-east, small EU traffic. We can keep POC in one region.
[01:15] Priya: Ok so rough throughput calc: 120 qps sustained with avg 160 tokens total implies X tokens/sec. We'll map that to GPU capacity in the bench. Any req concurrency limits on your side?
[01:28] Ethan: We cap client concurrency; the front-end multiplexes, but backend can hit higher concurrency. We can collect traces and token histograms — we'll send those.
[01:35] Priya: Perfect. For reserved capacity we usually propose sizing to handle 90-95% of expected sustained load with autoscale to burst for peaks. That keeps committed cost lower and still meets p95 latency SLO most of the time.
[01:50] Jara: What's the tradeoff versus just reserving more GPUs?
[01:53] Priya: Reserving covers cost predictability, but you pay for idle cycles. Burst (on-demand) can be used for short peaks and priced higher. Also important: warmup times and cache cold starts. If you rely heavily on sub-second p95, large bursts can still hit cold-start penalties unless we pre-warm or keep some standing capacity.
[02:12] Alex: Example: reserve N GPUs sized for steady-state; configure autoscale policy to add M GPUs when queue length > threshold for > 30s. Also set a maximum burst and a cooldown period. For POC we can propose reserve for 80-90% steady and allow a 2x burst cap.
[02:30] Mark: How do you handle fallback if burst can't satisfy a spike — degrade gracefully?
[02:34] Priya: We have three typical fallbacks: 1) Route to a lower-cost model variant (quantized or smaller architecture) with graceful quality regression; 2) Route to a different region where capacity is available; 3) Queue + rate-limit with a client-side retry strategy. We prefer option 1 for interactive apps.
[02:52] Sophie: From security perspective, if we go cross-region, how is data residency handled?
[02:55] Alex: For POC we can avoid cross-region; but if needed we can use encryption-in-transit and ensure logs/audit remain in the requested region. Private deployment options are possible for Prod.
[03:10] Priya: Bench plan: we'll run your traces against a few model variants: full fp16, int8-quantized, and a smaller family model. We'll measure p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and token cost. Success criteria: p95 < 500ms on the reserved+burst profile, cost per 1M tokens within your budget target, and no more than X% error/regression on a small eval set you provide.
[03:40] Mark: That aligns. Our business wants p95 under 500ms and avg cost below $Y per 1M tokens — I'll put a hard number in the doc.
[03:48] Ethan: About warmup — we use KV cache for code completions. How does cache behave across scaling events?
[03:55] Priya: KV cache (we sometimes transcribe it as K-V) is per inference shard. On autoscale up you'll have cold caches on new replicas; for that reason we recommend staggered warmup and a small standing pool to keep hot keys warm. Also prefix caching on the host side can help.
[04:16] Jara: For the POC, what's the recommended reserved GPU type? We use AWS g5dn or similar.
[04:22] Priya: For code workloads, A100/RTX6000 class or Ampere-like instances are good. For the bench we'll emulate with the GPUs in Redwood Dedicated; we'll pick a config that mirrors your infra (we can match instance family).
[04:35] Alex: Pricing: reserved commit monthly vs burst on-demand hourly. We'll send a POC pricing sheet with example cost calc for the recommended reserve+2x burst model.
[04:47] Mark: Good. On autoscale thresholds — what do you recommend for cooldown windows and queue thresholds?
[04:52] Priya: Typical: scale up when queue length > 20 requests for more than 30s, scale down after 3m of low utilization. But we'll tune on bench results; aggressive downscales can cause flapping. We also recommend smoothing with a moving avg of queue length.
[05:10] Ethan: If we have stateful sessions or KV cache, does autoscale cause session loss?
[05:14] Priya: Not if sessions are handled at the routing/proxy layer — you can keep session affinity for a short TTL. For short-lived stateless calls it's fine; for sessions we recommend sticky routing plus a small standing reserve.
[05:26] Sophie: Security checklist — we need SOC2 details, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integration.
[05:31] Alex: We'll share the SOC2 pack and KMS integration notes. For POC we can run with redwood-managed keys, but for Private you can bring your own KMS.
[05:42] Mark: Bench details — can Redwood run the bench in our account or do we run it and share results?
[05:48] Priya: Two options: we run from Redwood Dedicated in your region (with a test workload) or you run our benchmark harness in your account. For POC speed, Redwood-run initial bench is quickest; then we can replicate in your account for final verification.
[06:05] Alex: We'll need traces (Ethan will send), a token histogram, and a short eval set for quality checks. After bench we'll share: latency percentiles, GPU utilization traces, recommended reserve count, burst cap, and cost calc.
[06:18] Jara: Timeline?
[06:20] Alex: If we get traces by Thu (06-26), bench run by Mon/Tue (06-30/07-01), results and proposal by 07-01. Technical deep dive to discuss infra specifics the week after.
[06:33] Mark: Sounds good. One more — model variants: do you have pre-quantized builds and how much perf gain do you expect?
[06:40] Priya: We have quantized builds and runtime optimized kernels; int8 often gives 1.8-2.5x token throughput depending on model and GPU. We'll include those deltas in the bench report.
[06:52] Ethan: If we need private deployment later, how different will the POC be?
[06:56] Alex: POC identical in behavior; Private adds control plane and networking. We'll document any infra prerequisites. It may change warmup/cold behaviour slightly due to different networking.
[07:08] Mark: For fallback quality regressions, we need a way to measure user impact — do you support A/B style routing in the platform?
[07:14] Priya: Yes, rollouts and canarying are supported — you can route X% to a smaller model and monitor quality/regressions and rollback automatically. We'll instrument with eval prompts you provide.
[07:28] Jara: Ok let's recap next steps.
[07:30] Alex: Recap: Redwood will run bench, send pricing with reserve+burst plan, share SOC2/security docs, propose autoscale thresholds, and schedule deep dive. Nimbus to send traces and token hist.
[07:43] Mark: Agreed. Any blockers?
[07:45] Sophie: We'll need the security questionnaire answered before any cross-region testing; otherwise ok.
[07:51] Alex: No problem, we'll return that.
[07:54] Priya: One more note: for POC we recommend a 2-week run to capture multiple traffic patterns. That gives better confidence on autoscale tuning.
[08:04] Jara: Two weeks is fine.
[08:06] Alex: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the POC doc and proposed time for deep dive.
[08:14] Mark: Thanks.
[08:15] [call ends]
